title: SPOCK and European PGx networks
text:
Role: Work package collaborator
Networks: SPOCK consortium, COST Action CardioPharmGeneNet, Clinical Pharmacogenetics Implementation Consortium (CPIC)
Status: Ongoing since 2022

SPOCK is a multinational consortium on CYP2C19 genotype-guided antiplatelet therapy. I contribute Danish register and biobank data and take part in the methods work package. Through CPIC I co-authored the 2025 guideline on NAT2 and take part in the network’s working groups.

title: National pharmacogenetics pipeline
text:
Role: Member of the national clinical project group, appointed national expert
Lead: National Genome Center, with the Department of Molecular Medicine (Aarhus University Hospital) and MDx Core (Rigshospitalet)
Period: 2025 to 2027, under the National Strategy for Personalised Medicine
Scope: 24 drug-gene pairs where CPIC, DPWG and FDA agree
Collaborators: Peter Breining (Aalborg University Hospital and Aarhus University Hospital, clinical lead), Troels Korshøj Bergmann (University of Southern Denmark), Per Damkier (Odense University Hospital and University of Southern Denmark) and Niels Herluf Paulsen (Odense University Hospital)

Thousands of Danish patients have whole-genome sequencing done on clinical indication every year. The pharmacogenetic variants in those genomes are read once and then sit unused. Initiative 2.1 builds one national bioinformatic method that calls star alleles for CYP2C19, CYP2D6, CYP2C9, DPYD, TPMT, NUDT15, SLCO1B1, ABCG2 and UGT1A1 from the sequencing data, reports them as structured laboratory results, and shows the recommendation in the shared medication decision support system when a doctor prescribes one of the affected drugs.
I write the clinical recommendations for the drug-gene pairs together with the other clinical pharmacologists in the group, and I align the regional pharmacogenetic panel at MDx Core, Rigshospitalet, where I am clinical lead, with the national method so the two give the same answer.

title: Michael Asger Andersen
text:
Physician and clinical pharmacologist in training
I am a specialty registrar in clinical pharmacology at Bispebjerg and Frederiksberg Hospital, Copenhagen, with a PhD in medical science. I study whether pharmacogenetic testing and therapeutic drug monitoring change prescribing and patient outcomes. The data come from Danish nationwide health registers, the Copenhagen Hospital Biobank and prospective clinical trials.
Right now I run SAMSON-2, a nationwide N-of-1 trial on statin intolerance, and TDM-VISION, a drug monitoring project for ibrutinib and venetoclax in chronic lymphocytic leukemia. In parallel I link CYP2C19 and SLCO1B1 genotypes from the Copenhagen Hospital Biobank to clinical outcomes in nationwide registers, and I sit on the national project group that builds the pharmacogenetic pipeline under the Danish National Strategy for Personalised Medicine.
See all projects, the publication list or the CV as PDF.

title: About
text: I am a physician and specialty registrar in clinical pharmacology at Bispebjerg and Frederiksberg Hospital, Copenhagen. I trained as a doctor at the University of Copenhagen, did a PhD on infections in chronic lymphocytic leukemia at Rigshospitalet, and spent a year in cardiovascular clinical development at Novo Nordisk before returning to the hospital. My research combines Danish nationwide health registers, the Copenhagen Hospital Biobank and prospective clinical trials to test whether genotype-guided prescribing and therapeutic drug monitoring improve patient outcomes.

title: Biobank pharmacogenetics
text:
Role: Principal investigator
Data: Copenhagen Hospital Biobank genotypes linked to the Danish National Patient Register, the Prescription Register and the Civil Registration System
Status: Analyses ongoing
Collaborators: John R. Shorter (Roskilde University, statistical genetics), Morteza Vaez (Institute of Biological Psychiatry, Mental Health Centre Sankt Hans, PyPGx genotype calls) and Ole Birger Vesterager Pedersen (Copenhagen Hospital Biobank)

Guidelines recommend CYP2C19 testing before clopidogrel and SLCO1B1 testing before simvastatin, but Danish hospitals rarely test. This project uses existing genotypes from the Copenhagen Hospital Biobank to estimate what testing would have changed: how many patients carry actionable variants, what happened to them on the drug, and whether the result justifies routine genotyping. The analyses run in R with data.table on the Danish national research servers.

title: SAMSON-2
text:
Role: Sponsor and principal investigator
Design: Multicenter randomized controlled trial across 11 Danish cardiology lipid clinics
Status: Approved in CTIS (2025-524955-30-01), protocol paper submitted October 2026
Funding: Capital Region of Denmark, Bispebjerg Hospital research fund, Hørslev-Fonden
Sites: Bispebjerg and Frederiksberg Hospital (sponsor site), Herlev and Gentofte Hospital, Zealand University Hospital Roskilde, Holbæk Hospital, Odense University Hospital, Hospital of Southern Jutland (Aabenraa), Esbjerg Hospital, Aarhus University Hospital, Regional Hospital Central Jutland (Viborg and Silkeborg), Gødstrup Regional Hospital and Aalborg University Hospital
Collaborators: Christian Bork (Aalborg University Hospital, lipid clinic network), Morten Lamberts (Respons digital trial platform), Jonas Ghouse, Darrel P. Francis (Imperial College London) and Luke Pilling (University of Exeter)

Many patients stop statins because of muscle symptoms, but blinded trials show that most of those symptoms also appear on placebo. SAMSON-2 asks whether a patient’s own blinded comparison changes that. Participants in the N-of-1 arm go through six blinded 28-day blocks, three on rosuvastatin 20 mg and three on identical placebo, separated by 14-day washouts. They record symptoms daily in an app and receive their personal result at the end. The control arm gets guideline-directed titration by the lipid clinic. The primary question is whether the N-of-1 result leads to more patients on a statin one year later.
The trial builds on the UK SAMSON trial by Howard, Francis and colleagues (2020). Darrel P. Francis (Imperial College London) and Luke Pilling (University of Exeter) collaborate on design and genetics.



Trial flow. 160 participants are randomised 1:1. The N-of-1 arm alternates rosuvastatin and placebo in six four-week blocks and sees its own result at week 36; the control arm gets standard titration. The primary endpoint is read at month 15.

title: TDM-VISION
text:
Role: Principal investigator
Design: Prospective clinical study with pharmacokinetic sampling and exposure-response modelling
Status: Recruiting
Funding: Danish Cancer Society, DKK 2.3 million
PhD student: Cathrine Korsholm, supervised by Tonny Studsgaard Petersen and Mikkel Bring Christensen (Department of Clinical Pharmacology, Bispebjerg and Frederiksberg Hospital), Trine Meldgaard Lund (University of Copenhagen), Carsten Niemann (Department of Hematology, Rigshospitalet) and me
Collaborators: The Danish CLL network DALYCA and the Department of Clinical Pharmacy and Toxicology, Leiden University Medical Center

Ibrutinib and venetoclax are dosed by label, not by concentration, although exposure varies several-fold between patients. TDM-VISION measures drug concentrations in patients with chronic lymphocytic leukemia treated at Danish hematology departments and relates them to response, toxicity and dose changes. The goal is a monitoring algorithm that tells the clinician when a concentration should change the dose.
